en: The Heart Sūtra and the Diamond Sūtra are the two great essentials that summarize the Buddha’s teachings across all sūtras; they are the kings among dharmas. Furthermore, these two sūtras—the Heart Sūtra and the Diamond Sūtra—are the kings among sūtras themselves.
All those who possess the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and are thus designated as human beings, should likewise know and hear these sūtras.
Director: Those who possess faith do not oppose this; they also know how to copy, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others.
Whether they be monastics or laypeople, male or female, whether in a Buddhist monastery or a marketplace, anyone who does not know to respect these two sutras is certainly no human being.
Every person is fully endowed with it; every dharma is perfectly accomplished. Believing this very point, one realizes that sentient beings and Buddhas are entirely without distinction.
Huangmei used this to seal the mind; the *Platform Sūtra* used this to give voice.
The true eye of the Chan school is none other than this Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Today’s Wang Zhian and the Layman Pang of old each possess it.
The supreme cause of the "hand and eye" [of spiritual guidance]: when the sutras were expounded in the East at the Land of Lu, the teacher occupied the high seat;
when the Tripitaka was turned in the West at the Western Heaven, the peak of Gṛdhrakūṭa was ascended. Specifically, the general purport of these two scriptures is extracted and presented:

reading them is like water merging with milk, like a mustard seed entering a needle’s eye, or like a wish-fulfilling jewel—circular without end, continuous without interruption, requiring no artificial blending, and naturally threading together.
Indeed, it is thoroughly and perfectly luminous.

Because since beginningless kalpas those who have upheld, recited, and read [this sutra] have emerged to explain it to others—what is called "wondrously accords with the Buddha’s wisdom" and "skillfully enters the Buddha’s insight"—the Buddha originally granted permission to all good sons and good daughters based on this very capacity, not solely based on that capacity to grant it exclusively to bhikṣus. The words of the sutra are even more explicit: thus...
Manifesting in the form of a layman dressed in white robes to preach the Dharma for me—this is whom I have come to believe.
While staying at the Hermitage, I received the Dharma from Caoxi; this is a record of the meritorious encounter with Tan Zhenmo.
(Attached: An abridged summary of the *Heart Sūtra* transcribed by Pan Tan.
Written by Wang Qilong of Zhiai in Xiushui. Someone asked Prince Wang:
"You have recounted the general purport of the *Vajracchedikā*, which is indeed so. I do not know what the general purport of the *Heart Sūtra* is.
Prince Wang said: "It is difficult to speak of. The *Vajracchedikā* is one of the eight classes of Prajñāpāramitā. As for the *Heart*..."
The Sūtra, by means of few words, encapsulates manifold meanings and serves as the guiding framework for the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Within two hundred and sixty-eight characters of its title, it exhaustively gathers the vast and magnificent prose of six hundred fascicles. The essential core of the Buddha’s word reaches its ultimate limit here.
As for its general meaning, the essence of the Heart Sūtra and the essence of the *Vajracchedikā* are likewise no different.
There is no difference. Someone asks: "How is this clarified? It is said: The Sanskrit term *prajñāpāramitā* translates in Chinese as "wisdom reaching the other shore.
When the Buddha preached this sutra, his sole intention was to deliver sentient beings from their suffering and calamities.

The suffering and calamities of sentient beings are rooted in ignorance (*moha*). Ignorance is destroyed by wisdom, and through the union with True Suchness (*tathatā*), there arises inconceivable non-ignorance (*amoha*).
Through inconceivable perfuming of transformation, the five aggregates arise. Ignorance regarding these five aggregates constitutes the five turbidities;

they are also called the root-stumps of myriad sufferings, and also the ocean of existence within birth and death. Ordinary beings, attached to suffering, are ignorant and cling to existence, thus wandering through the sea of suffering.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle, fearing suffering, are ignorant and indulge in emptiness, seeking only for themselves to escape the sea of suffering, but not...
They are those who refuse to deliver others to cross together out of the sea of suffering. Clinging to existence, they are hindered by existence and do not attain sovereignty;
indulging in emptiness, they are hindered by emptiness and likewise do not attain sovereignty. They are entirely devoid of wisdom, or their wisdom is merely meager.

Consequently, for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, they fall into the suffering of segmented birth-and-death, they fall into the suffering of transformative birth-and-death, and they fall into the realms within and beyond the world.
The three sufferings, the five sufferings, and the eight sufferings—these are like layers of fine silk gauze, encompassing all coarseness and subtlety.

This single segment of wisdom-light, inherently possessed by every person and perfectly realized within each individual, is either submerged and unmanifest, or appears only partially rather than fully.
Thus, those who truly ascend to the other shore of Nirvana are rare indeed. Out of profound and deep compassion, our Buddha felt sorrow and pity; regarding this matter, he spoke...
At the time of Prajñāpāramitā, he was Avalokiteśvara, who had attained the power of great mastery and fearlessly bestowed gifts upon sentient beings;
he was called the foremost in wisdom, one who did not delight in the Hīnayāna, and was Śāriputra, who aroused the movement of compassion.

He showed people the method for escaping suffering and taught them the dharma for reaching the further shore. Avalokiteśvara possessed the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing and the Samādhi of Universal Illumination. Furthermore...

He possesses the Samādhi of Seeking Sound to Rescue from Suffering. Because he contemplates with sovereign mastery (*avalokita*), he is named "Sovereign" (*svayambhū*). His self-observation constitutes wisdom, distinguishing him from ordinary beings.
By practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, his practice and realization are far superior to those of the Hīnayāna.

Above, he shares the power of compassion with all Buddhas; below, he shares the aspiration of pity with all sentient beings. Thus, he is not only able to emerge himself from the ocean of suffering of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, he is able to turn back toward the realm of worldly toil to rescue and deliver sentient beings, so that they may together emerge from the sea of suffering.

If one examines his supernatural powers, their application is simple and direct; there is nothing else beyond this, for it is simply to perceive that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby delivering all from suffering and calamity.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are subsumed under the single category of ignorance (*avidyā*). When analyzed, they are termed form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Form encompasses the sense organs, the body, and the objective world; it occupies the first of the eighty-one categories in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and constitutes the first solid delusion—the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
Sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitute the delusions of empty luminosity, pervasive fusion, profound concealment, and inversion.

This subtle conceptualization takes the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pāra-tantra-citta*; the mind that clings to objects) as its intrinsic nature; it is the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). What is called the "form" is a thicket of transgressions, and the "mind" is the soot of thieves.
It is the root of all suffering; it can obstruct not only ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), but can also obstruct the worthy and the noble (*ārya*).
However, as the former Buddhas have said: "Delusive thoughts lack inherent nature; thus the five aggregates are like illusions and cataracts, unreal like flowers in the sky.

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s tranquil illumination encompasses empty space, penetrating to the very source and bottom. His insight that the aggregates are empty does not mean that the five aggregates exist;
rather, it is because the Bodhisattva perceives them through the lens of emptiness that the five aggregates appear to exist. Although the Bodhisattva thus illuminates them...
One sees them. How could one empty them? In reality, the five aggregates are originally non-existent; yet the Bodhisattva alone possesses this insight that perceives them as such.

This is precisely what constitutes the extinction of the five aggregates, and the dissolution of emptiness itself. What is called True Suchness (Tathatā) has neither beginning nor end, whereas ignorance (avidyā) has no beginning but does have an end.
As long as the five aggregates are not perceived through this insight, the two delusions of characteristics and perception arise and perish in confusion.

Birth and death continue without ceasing; this is called the ocean of afflictions (*kleśa*). When one can clearly perceive the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), then the single reality is eternally profound and quiescent, fundamentally devoid of birth and death.

All phenomena are perfectly interfused; this is called the realm of true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*). Within the ocean of afflictions, it is because of form (*rūpa*) that the sense faculties (*indriya*) arise.
Because of the sense faculties there are objects; because of objects there is consciousness; because of consciousness there are the twelve links of dependent origination.

There are the Four Noble Truths, the attainment of wisdom, birth and cessation, defilement and purity, increase and decrease, the dharmas of ordinary beings, and the dharmas of the Perfect Enlightenment Śrāvakas—these are all various kinds of obstructions, terrors, and inverted dreams and delusions.
Thus, both the ordinary and the holy are ablaze, revolving up and down like a waterwheel.
Even a slight cloud of impurity defiles the Great Clarity (*mahāviśuddha*). That is to say, if one is deluded, karma and suffering accumulate, and not a single person attains sovereignty.

Within the realm of true emptiness (*bhūtakoṭi*), because the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) do not exist, there are no six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Because there are no six sense objects, there are no six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*).

Because there are no six consciousnesses, there are no twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*). There are no Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*), no attainment of wisdom, and no birth.
Extinction. It is stainless, pure, and free from increase or decrease. There is no dharma of ordinary beings; there is no dharma of the *saṃbuddha-śrāvakas*.
There is no obstruction, no terror, and no mind of inverted dreams or delusions. The Buddha and sentient beings are one path, perfectly level. To mold existence is like shaping emptiness;

it is as easy as extending or contracting one’s arm. This is what is meant by: "If one awakens to this, the myriad sufferings cease; there is not a single thing that is not sovereign. The Buddha takes pity on ordinary beings.
For those of lesser ignorance, these two dharmas—form and emptiness—are employed as the vanguard for total dissolution, serving to reveal the six characters:
"Contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty. Furthermore, from within these six characters, the true meaning of this contemplation is further expanded into sixteen characters:
"Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. Form...

"Emptiness is not different from form" is intended solely to refute the ordinary person’s attachment to existence. "Form is not different from emptiness" is intended solely to refute the Hinayanist’s indulgence in emptiness.

"Form is identical to emptiness; emptiness is identical to form" is intended solely to demonstrate that emptiness is not a stubborn emptiness apart from the aggregates or a nihilistic emptiness—the partial emptiness of the Hinayana—but rather the mutual fusion of the aggregates and emptiness, which constitutes the identity of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. There is no...

Thus, not even a single thread of attachment remains. That which exists is the ultimate emptiness of the victorious meaning of the forest-array and sea-seal, the first principle emptiness, the twenty kinds of emptiness, and the true emptiness.
This is the empty characteristic of all phenomena; it is the divine elixir that truly cures all suffering.
It is the raft for crossing over the two deaths. This refers to what the Buddhas have taught: "The Dharma of emptiness destroys the perception of existence;
yet if one clings to emptiness, the Buddhas cannot transform such a person. This is it. It also refers to: "Of all phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I say they are empty;
they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. This is it. According to this, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
The Buddha-dharma is neither real nor false. Is it not that form is emptiness and emptiness is form? All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
they are like dew and like lightning—one should contemplate them in this way. Is this not the insight that the five aggregates are all empty?
In my attainment of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not the slightest dharma to be acquired. Is this not because there is neither ignorance nor acquisition?
I have no perception of a self or a person; I have no perception of a sentient being or a life-span. Even when my limbs were severed joint by joint, I never harbored anger or resentment.

Whether cut with a blade or anointed with fragrance, I viewed them as one and the same. What suffering or calamity could there be? To bring all sentient beings to *nirvāṇa*, yet in reality, there are no sentient beings.
Is birth and extinction not ultimate nirvāṇa? Is suchness immovable not sovereignty?
These two characters, "sovereignty," are the ever-shining light of prajñā, true thusness, and buddha-nature. Contemplating the dharma-realm with clarity, humans and devas possess this sovereignty;
those of the two vehicles possess this sovereignty; bodhisattvas of the stage of semblance and partial truth possess this sovereignty; and all Buddhas possess it.
This is sovereign mastery (*vaśitā*). Among all non-Buddhists, Māras, insects, and sentient beings, there are none who do not possess this sovereign mastery.

However, if one does not contemplate it, sovereignty remains hidden; wisdom is transformed into delusion (*moha*). If one contemplates it, sovereignty is revealed; delusion is transformed into wisdom.
Yet, even while contemplating, sovereignty is already present; even without contemplating, sovereignty is fundamentally present from the beginning. [The] multitude...
The Buddha is one who has attained mastery over birth; he is the "other shore" where afflictions have been swept away. Sentient beings are those who lack such mastery;
they are the "this shore" characterized by worldly entanglement. Thus, one clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby crossing over suffering to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, the three characters of "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanyin) encompass everything without exception. Moreover, these words of the Buddha are quintessential.
The essence of the essence; the core of the core. The quintessential meaning of the Heart Sutra is fully exhausted herein.
For sentient beings suffering in affliction who wish to study the profound *prajñā* practiced by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, how can they ultimately reach the other shore?
Those who fear the ocean of suffering of the five aggregates and seek to escape it shall not reach the other shore. While dwelling in the midst of the ocean of suffering...
Seeing through [the world], one realizes there is originally no sea of suffering; one should then contemplate ascending [to liberation], for only thus can one reach the other shore.

Those sentient beings who fear and avoid the sea of suffering of the five aggregates, treating it as something defiling, shall not reach the other shore. One must vow to enter the sea of suffering of the five aggregates first;
until not even a single sentient being has emerged from suffering, one vows not to attain *nirvāṇa* therein. Only then is one truly able to board [the vessel].
Wisdom that has reached the other shore is perfectly penetrating, vast, and immeasurable and boundless; this is for those who have skillfully studied the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
In short, it is not only the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara who, by means of this wisdom, reaches the other shore.
All who act as Bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara, equally ride upon this wisdom to reach the other shore.
It is not only those who provisionally dwell in the Bodhisattva vehicle, like Avalokiteśvara, who ride upon this single Buddha-vehicle of wisdom to reach the other shore.
All the Buddhas who appear during the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*, the present *Bhadrakalpa*, and the future *Tārakakalpa* have all reached the other shore by means of this wisdom.

It is therefore fitting that the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* selects the "Perfect Penetration" (*pratyavekṣā-āyatana*) and uniquely extols the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara as the means for escaping suffering and attaining liberation. How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! He brings about the fulfillment of the bodhicitta.
Avalokiteśvara is the most supreme. This entire *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of several million words, yet these two hundred and sixty-eight characters crown it all.
As a sacred and secret text, its exoteric and esoteric teachings, from beginning to end, fully encompass the three categories [of the sūtra structure].
From the passage "Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara" up to "deliverance from all suffering and distress" may serve as the introductory section (*nidāna*). Śāriputra’s form...
Arising not apart from emptiness and culminating in the true reality of non-falsity, this may be considered the orthodox teaching.

Thus, the section from "The Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-mantra" to the end may be considered the propagation. To elaborate on its meaning in detail: how could it be limited to eight divisions and six hundred fascicles?

It would almost require the ink of the oceans and the writing of the brushes to exhaust it; even the great trichiliocosm could not contain it. Yet, when its essence is condensed, it consists of these eight divisions.

Six hundred fascicles are condensed into two hundred and sixty-eight characters; these two hundred and sixty-eight characters are condensed into the sixteen characters, "Form is not different from emptiness";
these sixteen characters are condensed into the six characters, "Contemplating that the five aggregates are all empty";
these six characters are condensed into the three characters, "Avalokiteśvara. Retreating into the profound mystery, the more concise it becomes, the more comprehensive it is—like a precious jewel.
A silken net suspends a great maṇi jewel; drawing in all that exists throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time into this single pearl, not a single thing is lost.
Ten thousand rays of precious light interlace and weave through one another in a magnificent pattern, connected without confusion.

Were it not for the Buddha’s flowing forth from his wondrously luminous mind and his broad and long tongue, how could any later śrāvaka disciples have been capable of such a compilation? And as for those who receive and uphold this Heart Sūtra...
It is not that our Buddha, in his profound penetration of capacities and dispositions, singled out Avalokiteśvara and Śāriputra;

it was rather like the original intent of Subhūti acting as the primary recipient in the *Vajracchedikā* assembly—a case of the "pecking and hatching" [of the egg]. It is as if those sailing across the sea have lost their compass, wandering in the dark for the needle’s path and knowing no place of refuge.
If one investigates the *Heart Sūtra* to its ultimate conclusion, where does the place of refuge lie? It never departs from what is already possessed within the *Vajracchedikā*.

Upholding the contemplative wisdom of the six suchnesses, one sweeps away the empty flowers of the five aggregates. One manifests the single suchness of birth and Buddhahood and realizes the true mark of ultimate emptiness.
This is the perfection; this is the consummation. Prajñāpāramitā is the wisdom that reaches the other shore; there is no meaning beyond it.
What is here set forth by my own view is non-dual and indistinguishable from the general purport of the *Vajracchedikā*. It is equal.

To extrapolate from this: as Vimalakīrti said, "Sever all false views and the two extremes of existence and non-existence"; as the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says, "Whether it be existence or non-existence, one must depart from both";
as the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* says, "When perfect Bodhi is attained, one returns to the state of having nothing to obtain";

as the *Awakening of Faith* says, "Knowing that these are like flowers in the sky, there is immediately no cyclic existence"; and as the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "Sentient beings are attached everywhere; [the Buddha] leads them [out of their attachments]."
He caused them to attain liberation. Shaoshi said, "Vast and open—there is no sage. The *Platform Sutra* says, "Be free from form within form; be free from emptiness within emptiness.
Qingyuan said, "Even the Noble Truths are not to be practiced. Nanyue said, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent, yet defilement must not be allowed.
Yongjia said, "The hundreds of thousands of worlds are bubbles in the ocean; the sages and worthies of the three periods are like a flash of lightning. As for ordinary people...
This [teaching] is identical in its ultimate truth to the Heart Sūtra’s deconstruction of form and emptiness and the wisdom that reaches the other shore.
To contemplate in this manner is to realize that the entire Great Canon—the five periods and eight teachings—is of one substance and one intent. The sūtra is the very heart of the Buddha.
The Buddha-mind is itself the sutra; who can divide them into two? Wisdom and ignorance have fundamentally no different nature. This shore and the other shore are originally of the same source;
who can obstruct this? When deluded, one is bound for kalpas; upon awakening, it is but a single instant. Thus was it proclaimed from the Golden Mouth.
The Perfect and Sudden True Doctrine, which exhausts the Great Divinity and Great Clarity—the Peerless and Incomparable—is the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye;
it is precisely the Heart Sutra and the Diamond Sutra that embody this.
The Prince’s exposition of the general meaning of the *Heart Sūtra* is hereby concluded. Someone remarked: "Your words are indeed clear;

however, there are those who have not read the great *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, and it is unlikely they will fully understand [your summary]. What can be done? The Prince could not help but feel compassion in his heart.
There are aspects of the sūtra’s meaning that require indirect elucidation, while others need only be summarized for clarity. The *Heart Sūtra* is the very essence of the sūtras; it is the Heart.
In the sutra, it is like the sun in the heavens; for those of initial capacity, this skillful means is all the more precious for its discernment.

Furthermore, to summarize the general essence, it is said: "The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom is the compassionate vessel that reveals the Buddha-nature within sentient beings and ferries them across the ocean of suffering.
All sentient beings of the nine realms possess body and mind; the afflictions and calamities of body and mind are ten thousandfold in total.
Names do not transcend the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). If one can see through these five aggregates, they are from the very beginning nothing other than True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Yet, ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle are deluded and fail to open this eye of wisdom. Some cling to the five aggregates, grasping at form as being real form;
others fear the five aggregates, falling into a view of emptiness as a partial emptiness. Consequently, they remain perpetually confined within birth and death, and Bodhi remains far away. West.
Now, the Sage, out of compassion for those wandering in the ocean of suffering, employs the union of emptiness and form to illuminate the truth.

Fearing that their deep-seated obstructions would be difficult to remove, he first provides citations as evidence. He speaks of the Bodhisattva of Profound Prajñā, who was the Tathāgata Bhaisajyaguru (Light of Righteousness) in the past;
he addresses the Śrāvaka foremost in wisdom, who is a vessel of the Supreme Vehicle present before him. From—
With single-mindedness, one contemplates through the power of mastery (*svayambhū*), illuminating the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and declaring them all to be empty.

This causes one to know that form (*rūpa*) is not different from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), thereby dispelling the ordinary person’s clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*). That emptiness is not different from form awakens the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) from their attachment to the arid.
"Form is itself emptiness" reveals the Bodhisattva; by means of the five aggregates, one realizes ultimate *nirvāṇa*. "Emptiness is itself form" clarifies the three periods of time.
The Buddhas attain perfect, equal, and right enlightenment within the very five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). True emptiness is not illusory;

it simply cannot be involved with birth and death, defilement and purity, increase or decrease. All phenomena are nameless, and there is no lingering attachment to the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths or the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Birth and death are one and the same as awakening from a dream. How could there be any obstruction, terror, or inverted dreaming?
Ordinary beings and sages are equal; cause and effect are equal. How can one distinguish between birth-and-death, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas?
Only do not fall into emptiness or existence. When the single mind does not arise, you will spontaneously see that there is neither lack nor excess. All phenomena are without fault.

Without moving a step, you reach the other shore, in accord with the Great Being’s realization of Perfect Penetration. These two hundred and sixty-eight words [are contained] within the eighth [chapter].
Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā section: if the net is held by its main cord, there will be order and no confusion. This eighteen-character divine mantra is protected by all the myriad spirits;
it is like a royal decree that none fail to obey. Formerly, when a master artisan traveled to the West, demons and devils obstructed his path;
because he held only the Heart Sūtra, they dispersed as soon as he thought of it. Those who uphold it should purify their minds so that they are like empty space, employing the ten similes.

Sixth, as in the contemplation of the five aggregates: one views all beings with compassion as if they were an only child; through the cultivation of hearing and the practice of what has been heard, one cultivates the threefold contemplation within a single mind;
by means of the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena, one realizes the bodhi of the four wisdoms;

and one thoroughly understands that the essence of true emptiness is devoid of intrinsic nature yet arises through conditions, like a bright mirror in which both Han and Hu appear together. As for illusory forms arising through conditions, they lack intrinsic nature, just like a mirror.
Like images in a mirror, they originally do not exist; regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), there is not a single thing that accords with the mind, nor is there a single thing that obstructs it.
With great function unfolding in every direction, not even a mote of dust is moved. The cages of ordinary and small-minded practitioners are suddenly transcended through sustained care;

by setting a fixed term, one delivers others from suffering. Such spiritual response is boundless. Otherwise, one merely chants in vain following the sound until the tongue grows hair—what possible connection could there be? Great!
My mind is dull and difficult to enlighten; out of reverence, I have again composed this brief summary. To drive a stake into empty space—how can I avoid the transgression of slandering the Dharma?
To fashion a literary composition from mere wood—I must now privately confess and repent for these errors. Thus it is said.
The Heart Sūtra: It is the heart of all sūtras, and it is also the sūtra of the mind. Among all sūtras, it stands as a single sūtra unto itself.
The Heart Sūtra not only governs and encompasses the great body of the *Prajñāpāramitā* as its own sūtra, but it truly governs and encompasses all the sūtras of the entire Tripiṭaka as its sūtra.
For the Buddha appeared in this world due to the causal conditions of the one great matter; setting aside the deliverance of ordinary beings...

To claim that, beyond the universal deliverance from all suffering and distress, the Buddha harbors some separate or residual intention, is truly like driving a stake into empty space or seeking a celestial palace at the bottom of the sea.
When the Buddha taught all dharmas, he universally delivered all minds;
let the tongues of both the Chan and doctrinal schools extend a thousand fathoms—could there be any other opening for speech? This is what is meant by "expounding this sutra."

Among the magnificent works of recent times, none can compare with the Venerable Zibo’s Three Expositions on the Heart Sutra, Li Zhuolao’s Outline of the Heart Sutra, and the Great Master Lingfeng Su’s Commentary on the Contemplation of Mind in the Prajñāpāramitā. I have here provided a summary of their essential meaning.
I have not dared to include even a single passage [from other sources], precisely so that it may be shallow rather than profound;
this is a skillful means intended for readers to see directly into the Buddha’s mind, like opening one's fist to reveal the palm.

As for the eighty-one sections of the great *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, those who wish to comprehend its meaning already have the commentaries of past and present masters available. This was further noted by the Buddha’s disciple, Wang Qilong.
Regarding the general meaning of the Heart Sutra, the colophon states:

"Others have said that the confusion between Confucianism and Chan Buddhism is a source of concern for those who uphold the worldly way. You, wearing the robes of a Confucian yet discoursing on the Buddha, must provide a clarification;
otherwise, you will not only incur the reproach of 'interfering in another's path,' but will truly be held responsible for the charge of 'two roots. You cannot save yourself."
"What is the point of this incessant prattle? I replied to him: "To hear [the Way] in the morning and die in the evening" is the teaching of the Former Sage.
"This mind and this principle" is the teaching of the former scholars. Master Zou (Zi Yu) detested both the bifurcation of two roots and the leveling of them;
he likewise detested the stubborn adherence to a single side. The synthesis of Confucianism and Buddhism has long been clearly manifest throughout the world; it does not require the present day.
I am ashamed that my own wisdom is so meager and inferior.

To venture these words of a mere beginner is like placing a paper lamp beneath the two luminaries [the sun and moon], or striking a clay pot amidst the eight musical tones; how could it possibly have any substance?
It is merely a deception born of a contrary heart, a speech of fraud for the sake of fame. Yet, when I take up my brush with self-confidence, I feel a chilling reverence before the Buddha.
The Bodhisattvas and noble sages raised their heads to observe and reflect, not daring to tread upon even a single word of it.

Thus, as for those who wear Confucian robes yet speak of Buddhism while committing sins—those who disregard the law do so not because there are two fundamental principles, but because they are maliciously attached to one-sided views.
